pages.title: Week 4: AI-powered user acquisition
pages.subtitle: Graham Kennedy | One supplied lecture recorded on 12 October 2026 | 59m 04s

blocks.title: The lecture in one sentence
blocks.body: Let AI watch public signals, rank and verify who might need you now, and draft the first message; keep the human on choosing sources, checking every lead and sending every message.

blocks.title: Five points to remember
blocks.body:
1. Below $1M ARR, network and intros are still the strongest channel; signal-based outreach is the fourth (S1 09:16; slide 5).
2. Four steps: Watch, Rank, Verify, Reach. Think of it as a funnel: about 115 names became 5 worth contacting in his example (S1 12:53-17:35, 31:21; slides 7, 11).
3. Before a clear ICP, use signals as research: find repeated pain and ask, do not pitch. After ICP, look for fit plus a trigger and name the signal (S1 17:53-21:20; slide 8).
4. AI does the searching, ranking, research and first drafts. You verify every lead and send every message yourself, for roughly the first 500-1,000 drafts (S1 25:49-30:00, 45:38-48:10; slide 18).
5. Turn the prompt into a system: context files, reusable skills, orchestration and integrations, improved by your feedback each run (S1 48:12-54:15; slides 19-27).

blocks.title: Where MediMind stands
blocks.body: You already ran Prompt #1 in class (W1). It found seven related records and no prospect that passed all three verification tests. That is an honest result: hospital leaders in a small market leave few public traces. Activities 1-5 (pages 7-11) redo the lecture's exercises as MediMind, using the 8 October product explainer and the 22 September buyer-pain research.
Fast route: this page, page 4 for the before/after-ICP table, page 7 for our company brief, page 9 for our signal library, page 12 for this week's actions.

pages.title: Signals and the four steps
pages.subtitle: Lecture evidence | S1 approximately 09:16-17:35 | D1 slides 5-7

blocks.title: What a signal is
blocks.body: Observable evidence that someone may be ready to buy, convert or stay. Signals are no longer rare; acting on them well still is (slide 6). Everyone can see the same public signals, so they help you and your competitors equally (S1 13:17).

rows: Your own data: CRM, customer interviews, product analytics
The market: news, hiring, funding, reviews, regulation, forums
High: real behaviour in your product
More powerful and fairly easy to set up (S1 12:53)
Check the public places your buyers talk and act
New leaders and hires, funding and expansion, complaints in reviews. New leaders often have a mandate to change software (S1 14:12).
Pick the few signals that show a company must act now
Pain beats profile. Newest first. Keep a top 5. Someone buying in six months gets a light touch every few months (S1 15:52).
Prove the signal is real, recent and fits your ICP
Matches best customers; dated and linked; contact still there. Over time you learn which signals tell the truth (S1 16:17).
A short note that names the signal and asks
Name the signal, share one insight, ask for a meeting. Mentors can help with this step (S1 17:03).

blocks.body: His examples of external triggers: a regulation or compliance change, a major data breach for security products, or end-of-quarter pressure for sales software (S1 11:43-12:01).

pages.title: Before and after a clear ICP
pages.subtitle: Lecture evidence | S1 approximately 17:53-21:20 | D1 slide 8

blocks.title: The key idea
blocks.body: Outbound works best on top of a strong offer and a good fit. Early on, the list is a research hypothesis to test in real conversations, not a sales pipeline (slide 8).

rows: Public complaints, posts asking for help, app store reviews
Hiring, funding, leadership changes, public announcements
Pain is real, current, and they know it
ICP fit, sourced lead, warm or known contacts

blocks.title: What he said about each side
blocks.body:
Early: look across many complaints and conversations for something that repeats; over weeks and thousands of signals, a few hundred companies may surface. Use outreach to learn your positioning and offer, e.g. ten companies with ten different messages (S1 19:39-20:37).
Later: you already know the pain. Avoid tyre-kickers, decide which accounts the CEO calls personally, tailor messages and find the channels where buyers spend time (S1 20:37-20:51).

blocks.title: Why ICP clarity matters to the AI
blocks.body: Without an ICP the tool can only ask 'is this a pain I might solve?'. With a clear ICP it can check 'is this a good customer?'. The better your ICP and customer data, the more accurate the ranking and verification (S1 25:16-25:46).

pages.title: The Taskroom example
pages.subtitle: Lecture evidence | S1 approximately 21:30-34:10 | D1 slides 9-13

blocks.title: What he did
blocks.body: He ran the post-ICP prompt for a batch company, Taskroom, using only public information and its 500 Global materials. Claude chose its own signals (for example franchise HQs already paying for an answering service), found about 115 companies, then narrowed them: 13 to watch, 10 ranked, 5 verified as worth contacting (S1 21:57-31:55; slide 11). The run took about 15 minutes.

rows: The CARDS franchise database blocked web search. His prompt said: if blocked, use any other tool. Claude used the Firecrawl MCP to fill the search form and add about 75 more names with contact details (S1 31:57-33:13; slide 12).
Many useful sources are forms or databases, not search results.
For the 5 good-fit companies only, it researched websites, news and posts and built a profile of each (S1 33:21-34:06; slide 13).
Outreach starts from knowing them, not 'tell me what your company does'.
A spreadsheet with tabs Summary, Watch, CARDS results, Rank, Verify, Reach, Success, What to change.
The same structure the prompts ask for.

blocks.title: The outreach question (Dimitri, S1 27:00)
blocks.body: Participants receive many messages built on the same pattern ('your job post from this week...'). His answer: do not copy his draft. Build a voice document in your context folder (he trained his on a few hundred Gmail conversations, LinkedIn posts and presentations). Read every word of the first 500-1,000 AI drafts and correct it. Do not blast 50 people with a first AI message. A simple 'we are working on the same problem, can we connect?' may go further than a pitch. Best of all: warm intros.
For the many names that do not fit well, he suggests automated monitoring or lighter outreach, so you notice if they become a fit later (S1 30:53-31:21).

pages.title: Building the system
pages.subtitle: Lecture evidence | S1 approximately 40:37-58:10 | D1 slides 18-29

headers: You stay in the loop to
rows: Read every draft (first 250-500 on the slide; he says up to about 1,000)

blocks.title: Four layers (slide 19, a graphic he credits to someone else)
blocks.body: Context: files about your company, ICP, voice, competitors, so AI stops guessing. Skills: repeatable instructions, e.g. how to verify a lead. Orchestration: the AI decides which skills and agents to run for an outcome. Integrations: CRM, product analytics, email and especially customer interviews (S1 48:12-50:14).

blocks.title: How he runs it
blocks.body: One prompt becomes 10-15 skills and often 18-20 sub-agents, so he runs it overnight (S1 44:33-45:27). Most of his skills come from others or from AI, e.g. gtmskills.com; read them before use (S1 50:18). 'Build a system that prompts itself' (slide 22). His first setup needed 12-13 nights of runs and morning corrections before it was good (S1 51:53-52:20). His example company 'Tally' is invented; its folder layout is on slide 24. He now runs about a 20-agent marketing team (slide 27).

blocks.title: A free option: Google Workspace Studio (slide 29, S1 54:20-56:14)
blocks.body: On paid Workspace accounts. A point-and-click flow that runs on a schedule: extract context, filter signals, research, add leads to a sheet, summarize fit, draft emails, notify in Chat. He wakes up to 10-15 prospects, some good, some bad, and sometimes passes them to Claude to check.

A participant (Mark, S1 41:30) reported that Claude's signals matched what his team already tracks with Apollo and Clay, and that it found two existing paying customers, which suggests the targeting works. He found ranking and verification good and outreach weak. Chat answer on build vs buy: tools like Attio, Clay and Lemlist can be worth it; he buys most things but builds acquisition because it matters most.

blocks.title: Why start here
blocks.body: Both prompts begin with a company brief, and the lecturer's first homework is 'set up your GTM context' (slide 31). The same brief becomes the first context file. Sources: product explainer of 8 October (X1), buyer-pain research of 22 September (R1), your class run of 12 October (W1).

rows: MediMind, medimind.md. One tailored hospital operating system replacing disconnected hospital software, built on FHIR R4 (X1).
Private multi-specialty hospitals and hospital groups in Georgia. Owners and CEOs lead the purchase; clinical, operations, finance and IT evaluate (X1).
Target market, not yet a repeating customer pattern
Not documented in the notes reviewed. Write down why the anchor partner chose MediMind, in its own words, before running Prompt #2.
Anchor agreement with GeoHospitals, a 25-hospital network, implementation proceeding in stages (X1). Not 25 independent wins; no measured outcome numbers yet.

Next 10 hospitals: Phase 1 parallel evaluation included before any commitment, current software stays, price match for the agreed base scope, ongoing base-product development. First parallel version targeted about two weeks after scope, permitted data and readiness are agreed (X1).

500 Global B11 and its mentors; the anchor partner's relationships; the physician-led team's clinical network. A public project list is a map, not a connection (W1).
Introductions and direct meetings first. LinkedIn is the lecturer's default for Western B2B (S1 10:42); hospital owners in Georgia may not be reached that way.

blocks.body: Keep the phases separate in every field: Phase 1 is the connected base system; workflow AI and the proactive AI brain are later, separately agreed phases (X1).

blocks.title: What the result tells us
blocks.body: Not 'the tool failed'. It suggests that for a small hospital market, public pain signals are scarce and the useful output is a short map of people and organizations to learn from. Mark's run worked because his buyers leave public traces (hiring, analytics) and he had a paying-customer list to calibrate against (S1 41:30-44:04). We have one anchor partner, so calibration data is limited.

blocks.body:
1. Fill the missing 'why they bought' field from the anchor partner experience.
2. Run Prompt #2 with the trigger signals on page 9, and the 'if blocked, use another tool' instruction the lecturer added (S1 32:17-32:27).
3. Add a Georgian-language source list (news, job boards, official pages) so the search is not English-first.

pages.title: Activity 3: our signal library
pages.subtitle: MediMind working draft | Adaptation of Watch and Rank | D1 slides 6-8 | built on R1 buyer pains

blocks.title: How this table was built
blocks.body: Each row is one of the six provisional buyer pains in R1, with the trigger R1 says to test. The new column asks the lecturer's question: can we see this trigger from outside? All rows are hypotheses until hospitals confirm them.

rows: 1. Losing money between care and paperwork
Rejected claims, a weak financial month, unexpected cost differences
Rarely. Mostly internal; reimbursement news shows policy pain, which software may not fix
2. Staff time lost to repeated work
Partly: repeated job posts for nurses, coordinators, registry or billing staff
3. No timely, trusted picture for leadership
Disputed board numbers, a new hospital joining the group
Partly: acquisitions, new branches and group expansion in the news
4. Staff manually connecting the patient story
Near misses, delayed decisions, handoff complaints
Rarely. Sometimes in quality projects or conference talks (W1 found C/Can)
5. Cannot change at the speed needs change
Costly change request, failed integration, contract renewal
Partly: tenders, IT job posts, a vendor change announced
Audit, new reporting rule, security incident
Yes for rules: Ministry and State Audit Office publications

blocks.title: Ranking rule for MediMind
blocks.body: Score each signal on pain (is one of the six pains clearly present?), fit (private, multi-specialty, independent buying organization) and freshness (last 90 days). Pain beats profile; keep a top 5 only (slide 7). A new owner, CEO or medical director is a strong trigger because new leaders often have a mandate to change systems (S1 14:12).

Internal signal to add: what the anchor partner's staff actually adopted and asked for in Phase 1. It is the highest-trust signal we have. Use only aggregate, permitted facts; no patient data or hospital-confidential information goes into external AI tools.

pages.title: Activity 4: verify, then reach
pages.subtitle: MediMind working draft | Adaptation of Verify and Reach | D1 slides 7-8, 18 | nothing here is to be sent automatically

rows: One of the six pains, said by the hospital's own staff in a work context
Not only a tariff, payer or staffing-supply problem
R1 boundary; W1 dropped one lead for this
A separate buying organization, not another branch of a group already counted
Our bottleneck is evaluations beyond the anchor
A real introduction or professional invitation exists
Lecture: warm intros beat cold messages (S1 29:23)

blocks.title: Reach: ask, don't pitch (early-stage column, slide 8)
blocks.body:
To a CEO or owner, after an introduction: 'When you prepare for a management meeting, how long does it take to get numbers everyone trusts, and where do they come from today?'
To a medical director: 'When a patient moves between departments, what does your team still have to chase by phone or paper?'
To a finance lead: 'Which corrections between care records and billing take your team the most time each month?'
Each opener names one pain from R1 and asks for a real example. None mentions AI or promises a result.

blocks.title: Our human-in-the-loop rules (from slide 18 and S1 45:38-48:10)
blocks.body: AI may search, rank, research and draft. A person checks every lead, reads every word, and sends every message personally. Start a voice file from your own past messages to hospital leaders, as the lecturer did with his email and posts. Introduce the parallel evaluation only after the hospital has confirmed a pain.

blocks.title: Where it lives
blocks.body: Keep it next to the existing marketing workspace (MediMind Landing Page/marketing), which already holds R1, the evidence register and the interview guide. Link to the canonical positioning files instead of copying them.

blocks.title: A small weekly loop
blocks.body: Monday: run a signal scan (Prompt #2 or a Claude Code skill) over the Georgian source list. Tuesday: verify the top 5 by hand with the five tests. Then: ask the network for introductions to those that pass. Friday: update outcomes.md and tell the system what it got wrong, as the lecturer did for 12-13 nights (S1 51:53). Workspace Studio (slide 29) is a free way to schedule the scan.

Guardrails in every file: Phase 1 only in the offer; no clinical, revenue or cost promises without hospital evidence; no patient or confidential hospital data in external tools; branches under one buying decision count once.
